guard: a seat spawned with an initial prompt submits it as its first turn, exactly once
why: The shipped defect had a shape that reads as working code: the launch spec was built, the seat
joined the roster, the persona loaded, and the only thing missing was the turn nobody was
watching for. So the mutation is the same shape rather than a broken build. It carries the
prompt over the env exactly as the fix does and then declines to submit it, which is what the
connector did for its whole life before this change.
IT TARGETS THE PLUGIN, NOT THE LAUNCH SPEC, because the launch-spec half is the half that could
already be proved by reading. A spec cell reddens on a one-line revert and nobody would doubt
it. The half worth grading is the one that needs a session, a mesh join, and a turn boundary to
observe at all, and it is the half where a passing suite could plausibly be measuring the
connector's env write rather than an actual turn.
THE ARM-B CONTROL IS WHY THE KILL MEANS WHAT IT SAYS. Arm A alone would also be satisfied by a
plugin that prompts at boot unconditionally, and such a plugin would waste a turn on every seat
that never asked for one. Arm B boots the same plugin with the carrier absent and requires
silence, so the two arms together pin the turn to the prompt rather than to the boot.
SPECIFIER BOUNDARY: the suite imports `../src/plugin.js` and `../src/extension.js` and runs
under tsx, so the bytes mutated are the bytes executed. No dist is built by the command, and no
`afterRestore` is needed to undo one.
THE BOOT PROMPT IS THE ONE INPUT THIS CONNECTOR CANNOT REDELIVER. An inbox batch that is not driven
stays in the inbox and arrives on the next wake; the spawn prompt lives in one variable in one
process, so a path that clears it without submitting it destroys it. B1 to B3 are about that loss.
B1 IS THE DEFECT AS IT SHIPPED: the boot task cleared the flag and then called drive, so a natively
submitted prompt that had already made the session busy sent drive down its early return and the
operator's prompt was gone, with nothing holding it and no later wake looking for it. A reviewer
reproduced that against the real plugin, broker held down so the boot task parked, before the cell
existed. B1 restores exactly that ordering.
B2 ASKS THE OPPOSITE QUESTION, and it is needed because B1 alone would pass an implementation that
never clears the flag at all: keeping the text after a successful submission turns every later
readiness event into a second boot turn.
B3 REMOVES THE RETRY RATHER THAN THE KEEP. Holding the text is only half the repair, since
something has to come back for it; with the predicate dead the text survives and is never carried.
THE COMPLETION MARKER IS THE PART COMMON TO BOTH EXITS, deliberately. It used to be the PASSED
line, so a mutated run that failed correctly printed FAILED, the marker never matched, and every
mutation here graded INCONCLUSIVE rather than KILLED. A marker that only appears on success cannot
distinguish a suite that caught the defect from a suite that died before reaching the cell.
B1 HAD TO BE RE-AIMED once the wake nudge was carried, and the reason is worth keeping. As first
written it only restored the old clear-then-drive, and it SURVIVED: `drive` now holds an override
it cannot submit, so the very text B1 destroys is caught by the general repair and the mutant
stopped modelling a loss. That is the class fix subsuming an instance, not a coverage gap. B1 now
discards the held text as well, which is what the code did before either repair existed.
B4 AND B5 ARE ARM D, AND THEY ARE TWO CELLS BECAUSE THEY ARE TWO CLAIMS. A wake arriving before
the boot prompt's drive used to starve both of them permanently: the boot text was carried only
when the wake slot was empty, so a parked nudge sent the boot drive down the floor's early return
and back into the slot, and emptying the slot needed the very submission the floor had refused.
Silent and permanent, and a REGRESSION against the base, which lost only the wake and still
submitted the boot. Reproduced live against this plugin before the arm existed.
B4 restores that carry condition, so the deadlock comes back and the boot is never submitted. B5
leaves the carry alone and takes the COMPOSITION away instead: the boot then goes out on its own
while the nudge is discarded by the slot's own success clear, which is the half-repair that would
pass an arm graded on the boot alone. Neither mutation touches arms A, B or C, so each reddens the
arm-D cell it names and nothing earlier.

mutations.name: the boot drive is dropped, so the prompt is carried over the env and then never submitted
mutations.expectRed: a boot prompt drives a turn without any peer traffic
mutations.cell: a boot prompt drives a turn without any peer traffic
mutations.note: The defect as it shipped, minus the parts that were never the problem. Everything around it survives: the connector still writes the carrier, the plugin still reads and clears it, the session is still created, the mesh is still joined, and the seat still answers a directed message seconds later. Only the first turn is missing, which is exactly how the drop escaped notice for as long as it did.

mutations.name: B1 the boot task clears the prompt before it is submitted, so a native turn that made the session busy sends drive down its early return and the operator's prompt is destroyed
mutations.expectRed: boot-race: the boot prompt survived the native turn and was submitted after it

mutations.name: B2 the prompt is never cleared once submitted, so every later readiness event issues the boot turn again
mutations.expectRed: no later readiness event re-issues the boot prompt

mutations.name: B3 the pending predicate goes dead, so the boot text is kept but nothing ever comes back to carry it
mutations.find: const bootPending = (): boolean => bootReady && bootPrompt !== undefined;
mutations.expectRed: boot-race: the boot prompt survived the native turn and was submitted after it

mutations.name: B4 the boot text is carried only into an empty wake slot again, so a focus @mention that lands before the boot drive starves the boot, the wake and every later connector-submitted turn
mutations.replace: const boot = carried === undefined && bootPending() ? bootPrompt : undefined;
mutations.expectRed: boot+wake: the boot prompt was submitted even though a wake arrived in front of it
mutations.cell: boot+wake: the boot prompt was submitted even though a wake arrived in front of it
mutations.note: The wedge as reviewed: no error, no retry, the seat online throughout. Everything else in the arm still happens: the seat joins, enters focus, the mention is delivered and acked at ingest, and only the two turns are missing.

mutations.name: B5 the boot turn stops composing with the wake it is carrying, so the boot goes out alone and the nudge is discarded by the slot's own success clear
mutations.find: const text = boot !== undefined && carried !== undefined ? `${boot}\n\n${carried}` : (boot ?? carried);
mutations.expectRed: boot+wake: the wake that arrived first was delivered rather than parked into the boot
mutations.cell: boot+wake: the wake that arrived first was delivered rather than parked into the boot
